displayTitle: The Erdős similarity conjecture: geometric patterns

scope.note: Reviewed against the October 5 introduction, theorem 1: for every fixed q in (0,1) and η in (0,1), a compact subset of [0,1] of measure greater than 1−η avoids x+s{qⁿ:n≥1} for every x and every nonzero signed s. The set may depend on q. This resolves the reported geometric-progression case, not the full conjecture for arbitrary infinite sets or a simultaneous all-ratios statement. The September 25 companion is the dyadic instance. Scope review does not assess the proof.

originalQuestion: Given any infinite set E of real numbers, can one find a set S of positive measure containing no similar copy of E? Erdős states this as Problem 4.33.7* in his 1974 congress problem list and reduces attention to countable sets whose sole limit point is 0, with 0 itself excluded.
modernQuestion: A set A is measure universal if every Lebesgue-measurable set of positive measure contains x+sA for some real x and nonzero real s. The full conjecture says no infinite A is measure universal. The geometric case asks whether, for each fixed q in (0,1), the sequence G_q={qⁿ:n≥1} is nonuniversal.
questionDifference: The 1974 question already concerns all infinite real sets and geometric similarity; affine notation makes the quantifiers explicit. Family 084 treats geometric null sequences only. Its reported conclusion strengthens positive measure to a compact subset of [0,1] of measure arbitrarily close to one, excludes every translation and every nonzero scale of either sign, and allows the avoiding set to depend on q. Avoiding almost every placement, avoiding a two-fold sumset, or allowing bi-Lipschitz distortion answers a different question.

conceptualOrigins.label: Finite-pattern embedding in positive-measure sets; predates the 1974 question (exact priority not established here)

firstFormulation.label: 28 June 1974: congress presentation recorded in the published problem list

attribution: Erdős explicitly posed the general avoidance problem in his 1974 congress problem list. The name identifies its proposer, rather than every ingredient in the later geometric case. Falconer and Eigen independently settled slowly decaying sequences; Bourgain supplied an additive branch; Kolountzakis developed probabilistic avoidance and almost-everywhere results. Feng, Lai and Xiong showed how changing the allowed maps changes the answer. This account identifies a printed 1974 formulation, not the earliest private discussion. The finite-pattern precursor is often attributed to Steinhaus, but the precise original scope has not been independently checked here.

contributors.name: Paul Erdős
contributors.contribution: Posed the general infinite-set avoidance problem and recorded its reduction to sequences approaching zero.

contributors.name: Kenneth Falconer and Stanley Eigen
contributors.contribution: Independently proved nonuniversality for positive decreasing sequences whose consecutive-term ratio tends to one.

contributors.name: Jean Bourgain
contributors.contribution: Proved nonuniversality for sums of three infinite sets, opening a branch based on additive structure.

contributors.name: Mihail N. Kolountzakis
contributors.contribution: Developed probabilistic avoidance criteria and sets excluding almost every affine placement of any infinite pattern.

contributors.name: De-Jun Feng, Chun-Kit Lai and Ying Xiong
contributors.contribution: Showed that fast-decaying sequences embed into every positive-measure set if bi-Lipschitz maps are allowed.

contributors.name: N. Mora Cuellar, A. Iosevich, N. Kulkarni, I. Rojas Aravena and A. Yavicoli
contributors.contribution: Reported nonuniversality for sums or differences of a geometric null sequence and any infinite set in a 2026 preprint.

uncertainty: The 1974 archive scan contains two neighboring papers: the similarity problem is in Problems, pp. 203–204, specifically Problem 4.33.7* on p. 204, not in the preceding Remarks on some problems in number theory. Its footnote dates the problem-session presentation to 28 June 1974; the publication gives no exact publication day. No first-private-formulation claim is made. The 1920 Steinhaus attribution is common in later research, but the original paper was not retrieved, so conceptual origins remain undated. Falconer and Eigen were checked through an institutional bibliographic record and the later primary Feng–Lai–Xiong paper; their original full texts were unavailable. The 2026 two-fold-sumset result is a preprint. The OpenAI introduction and history section were read for scope and context; proofs and independent acceptance were not assessed.

events.title: Positive measure forces every finite pattern
events.description: Near a density point, a positive-measure set is sufficiently full to contain a small affine copy of any prescribed finite set. This is the finite principle whose infinite extension becomes the question.
events.relationNote: A conceptual precursor, not an infinite-set theorem.
events.uncertainty: Later accounts often credit Steinhaus’s 1920 paper; its original scope was not checked, so this milestone is undated.

date.label: 28 June 1974: congress presentation recorded in the published problem list

events.title: Erdős asks whether every infinite pattern can be avoided
events.description: Problem 4.33.7* asks for a positive-measure set containing no similar copy of a prescribed infinite real set. The printed problem already notes the reduction to a countable set approaching zero.
events.relationNote: The shift is from a theorem about finite patterns to a proposed obstruction for infinite patterns.
events.uncertainty: The exact day dates the presentation recorded in a footnote, not publication or the first private discussion.

events.title: Slowly decreasing sequences can be excluded
events.description: Falconer and Eigen independently prove nonuniversality when a positive decreasing sequence tends to zero with consecutive-term ratio tending to one. A fixed geometric ratio q<1 lies outside this hypothesis.
events.relationNote: This settles a class of sequences while leaving the geometric benchmark separate.
events.uncertainty: Original full texts unavailable; the theorem and independent attribution were checked in the later primary Feng–Lai–Xiong paper.

events.title: Adding infinite sets supplies another route
events.description: Bourgain proves that the sum of three infinite real sets is not measure universal. This exploits additive structure rather than a slow-decay condition on a single sequence.
events.relationNote: An additive branch addresses a different class of infinite patterns.

events.title: Almost every placement can be blocked
events.description: Kolountzakis constructs positive-measure sets avoiding almost every affine placement of any infinite pattern and proves additional gap criteria for total avoidance. A measure-zero collection of surviving parameters may still contain placements.
events.relationNote: Probabilistic avoidance supplies substantial progress; almost everywhere is weaker than everywhere.

events.title: Allowing controlled distortion reverses the geometric answer
events.description: Feng, Lai and Xiong prove that fast-decaying sequences, including every G_q, embed into any positive-measure set by a bi-Lipschitz map. The map need not apply one constant scale to all points.
events.relationNote: A parallel variant shows why the rigidity of similarity matters.

events.title: A geometric summand helps exclude larger patterns
events.description: Mora Cuellar and collaborators report that sums or differences of a geometric null sequence and any infinite set are nonuniversal. Avoiding these larger patterns does not imply avoidance of the single geometric sequence.
events.relationNote: The preprint extends the additive branch to two summands, one geometric.
events.uncertainty: Preprint result; this account does not independently assess its proof.

date.label: 6 October 2026 release; geometric manuscript dated 5 October

events.title: The release reports avoidance for each geometric ratio
events.description: OpenAI reports compact subsets of [0,1] with measure arbitrarily close to one avoiding every translation and nonzero signed dilation of G_q, for each fixed q. The set may depend on q. The companion manuscript handles q=1/2.
events.relationNote: The reported claim addresses the single-sequence gap; neither the sumset nor bi-Lipschitz branch is asserted to be equivalent.
events.uncertainty: Reported mathematical claim; no independent proof assessment. The full conjecture for arbitrary infinite sets is outside its scope.

questionPlainLanguage: Can a set occupy almost all of an interval yet contain no translated or scaled copy of an infinite geometric pattern, such as ½, ¼, ⅛, …? One placement must fit every term, however far down the sequence it lies.
questionSummary: Can almost a whole interval avoid an infinite geometric pattern?
claimSummary: the geometric case, for every fixed ratio
questionFormal:
Write $G_q=\{q^n:n\geq1\}$, where $0<q<1$. An affine copy is $x+sG_q$ with $x\in\mathbb R$ and $s\ne0$; negative $s$ allows reflection. The geometric case asks for a positive-measure set containing no such copy.

The stronger statement reported by OpenAI is: for every $q,\eta\in(0,1)$, there exists compact $E_{q,\eta}\subseteq[0,1]$ with

$$m(E_{q,\eta})>1-\eta$$

such that

$$\forall x\in\mathbb R\;\forall s\ne0\;\exists n\geq1:\quad x+sq^n\notin E_{q,\eta}.$$

Here $m$ is Lebesgue measure. The order of the quantifiers matters: $E_{q,\eta}$ may depend on $q$. The full Erdős similarity conjecture replaces $G_q$ by any infinite subset of $\mathbb R$.
whyItMatters:
Positive measure expresses size without requiring a set to contain an interval. Even a fragmented set of positive measure contains a translated, scaled copy of every finite pattern of real points. Asking for an infinite pattern tests how far this powerful finite principle extends. Fitting longer and longer pieces does not automatically provide a single translation and scale fitting every point.

Geometric sequences make the boundary especially sharp: their points approach a limit at a fixed ratio, unlike the slowly decaying sequences covered by early results. Moreover, permitting a bi-Lipschitz deformation makes geometric sequences unavoidable again. The problem therefore probes both what “large” means and how rigidly a “copy” must preserve the pattern.
illustrativeExample: For $q=1/2$, the pattern is $G_{1/2}=\{1/2,1/4,1/8,\ldots\}$. Moving, shrinking or reflecting it preserves one common ratio. Only five terms are drawn. The hollow square marks the limit, which is not itself a term.
historicalHook: A set can contain every finite piece of a pattern without admitting the whole infinite pattern.
whatAIClaims:
OpenAI reports compact sets $E_{q,\eta}\subseteq[0,1]$ of measure greater than $1-\eta$ that avoid every affine copy of $G_q$, for each fixed $q\in(0,1)$ and each $\eta\in(0,1)$. Translations are arbitrary; dilations may be positive or negative. The October 5 manuscript treats all fixed geometric ratios, while the September 25 companion treats the dyadic case $q=1/2$.

The introduction describes an open complement of small measure that meets every placement. Its proposed probabilistic mechanism uses a finite routing tree to control the number of scale tests. This is the manuscript's reported approach, not a proof assessment by this site.
whatRemainsOpen: The claim does not resolve the conjecture for arbitrary infinite sets, including general rapidly decaying sequences. Nor does it assert one positive-measure set avoiding all geometric ratios simultaneously: a different set may be constructed for each ratio. Bi-Lipschitz copies remain possible by the earlier Feng–Lai–Xiong theorem, because those maps can distort the pattern rather than apply one common scale. Independent assessment of the 2026 proofs and their acceptance is outside this historical account.
